author: John of Damascus
occasion: John of Damascus writes in response to a request to explain what a human being is, offering a concise account of human nature in terms of the four humors, their bodily seats, and the anatomy of the head.
argument: A human being is defined as a rational, mortal living creature capable of intellect and knowledge, composed of four elements: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile. Each humor has a bodily seat and produces a distinct temperament: blood makes people cheerful and ruddy, yellow bile makes them quick and bold, black bile makes them sluggish and timid, and phlegm makes them sorrowful and forgetful. The humors also dominate successive stages of life: blood in childhood, yellow bile in youth, black bile in maturity, and phlegm in old age. The temple of the head is the ruler of the body, and the brain receives power and thought from the liver; the soul dwells in the brain. The work also describes the skull's sutures and the brain's membranes and parts, contrasting the brain with marrow.

outline.move: The letter opens with a definition of the human being as a rational mortal animal and lists the four humors with their bodily locations.
The author describes the temperaments produced by each humor and the humor that predominates at each stage of life.
The author explains the hot/cold and wet/dry qualities associated with each age based on the dominant humor, the temple's role as ruler of the body, and the anatomy of the skull and brain.
The author contrasts the brain with marrow, states that the body is composed of four elements because it contains the four humors, and locates each humor more precisely.

key_terms.sense: The four basic components of the human body: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile.
The humor located in the heart, warm and moist and sweet, producing cheerfulness and a ruddy complexion.
The humor located in the brain and chest, cold and moist, producing sorrow, coldness, and forgetfulness.
The yellow bile located in the liver and stomach, warm and dry, producing boldness and anger.
The black bile located in the spleen and loins, cold and dry, producing sluggishness and timidity.
The temple of the head, identified as the ruler of the body.
The brain, which receives power and thought from the liver and where the soul and the depth of thoughts reside.
The soul, which dwells in the brain along with the depth of thoughts.
The three membranes surrounding the brain.
The sutures or seams of the skull, of which there are normally five, though a single-sutured skull is always healthy.
The marrow, contrasted with the brain as dirty and bloody.
